title: Patanjali's eight limbs
hookLine: Patanjali's yoga has eight limbs, from how you treat others to absorption (Yoga Sutras 2.29)
carry: yoga begins with how you treat people

lines: ON A GYM SCHEDULE: A MAT AND POSES.
IN THE SUTRAS: ONE ITEM ON A LIST.
cards: On a gym schedule, yoga means a mat and a set of poses: downward dog, a warrior, a long lie on the floor at the end.
Then open an old Sanskrit text called the Yoga Sutras, credited to a teacher named Patanjali, and look for the poses. Posture is there, and the advice is brief: sit steady and at ease.
But it's one item on a list, and it isn't the first. The list has eight items. The book calls them limbs.
And the first two have nothing to do with stretching at all.

teach.b: Ashtanga: eight limbs. In sutra two twenty-nine, Patanjali names them in order. Yama, restraints.
Niyama, observances. Asana, posture. Pranayama, the regulation of breath.
Pratyahara, drawing the senses inward. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation.
Samadhi, absorption. The very next sutra spells out the restraints: not harming, truthfulness, not stealing, sexual restraint, and not grasping.
Kept everywhere, at every time, in every circumstance, the book adds, they become a great vow. Then the observances: cleanliness, contentment, discipline, study of oneself, and devotion to the Lord.
Before a single pose, this yoga asks how you treat people and what you do with your days.
Only then does the body sit down, steady and at ease, and the breath get attention.

Then the list turns inward, until in the last three limbs, which the book calls more inward than the first five, attention narrows to one point, flows there, and is absorbed. Readers take the shape in more than one way.
Some teachers read it as a ladder, each limb resting on the one below. Others lean on the word itself: limbs, like the arms and legs of one body, growing together rather than climbed and left behind.

The text leaves room for both. This week walked through Sufi and Muslim ways: watchfulness, al-Ghazali's crisis, solitude in the crowd, the retreat, the Mevlevi, prayer's rhythm. Today the road crosses into Hindu ways.

how: Students of classical yoga learn Patanjali's eight limbs as a path that begins with ethical restraints and observances, moves through posture and breath, and turns inward toward concentration, meditation and absorption; teachers differ on whether the limbs are steps or parts practiced together.

o: Patanjali's eight-part path, from ethics to absorption

games.q: you want to begin yoga the way Patanjali's list begins. where do you start?
o: with posture: get the body right first.
with the breath: slow it down.
with restraints: how you treat others.
games.why: the list opens with yama, restraints like not harming and truthfulness. posture comes third, breath fourth.

practice: Go down the list one limb to a breath, inside or in a whisper: restraint, observance, posture, breath, turning inward, concentration, meditation, absorption.
Then go back to the top and do it again, slower, noticing which limb feels near today and which feels far away, without fixing anything.

wordCard.voice: Ashtanga. Eight limbs, the shape of Patanjali's yoga in the Yoga Sutras: from how you treat others, through body and breath, inward to absorption. Today's word.
